extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and writers interested in post‑colonial literature, language politics, and decolonial creative practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for authors and critics about language choice, cultural representation, and the political role of literature in post‑colonial / African contexts. Emphasises whether to write in indigenous languages or hegemonic European languages and the consequences of that choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language choice: local language vs major European language
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the author choose to work in a local language or a major European one? (Margulis: "Does the author choose to work in a local language or a major European one?")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers tradeoffs: writing in a European language may gain international recognition and financial reward but risks cutting the writer off from their society's common experience; writing in a mother tongue may forego world‑market appeal but supports mass literacy and cultural rootedness. Evaluate intended audience, purpose, and consequences for cultural transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation practices and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: If the work is in a local language, how does it get translated and by whom? What might the translation have done to the work? (Margulis's questions about translation.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess translator identity, fidelity, and how semantic processes of abrogation/deformation or appropriation/reformation occur. Consider context of loaned terms and whether translation preserves, distorts, or appropriates cultural meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language as carrier of culture / 'language exists as culture'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Language as communication and as culture are then products of each other... Language carries culture, and culture carries... the entire body of values by which we come to perceive ourselves" (Decolonising the Mind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate texts for how linguistic choices transmit histories, values, aesthetics and shape collective perception and consciousness. Judge authenticity and cultural specificity via linguistic practices (vocabulary, idiom, orature forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding or perpetuating 'neocolonial mentality' through language
rubrics_metrics.description: To write fiction in English is to 'foster a neocolonial mentality' (Ngũgĩ's assertion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative lens: does the use of a hegemonic language in the text reproduce colonial hierarchies, alienation, or dependency? Anti‑pattern: uncritical adoption of coloniser's linguistic norms that reinforce imperialist values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing in indigenous languages as political resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing in African languages is characterized as 'a blow to imperialism' and part of reconnecting with revolutionary anti‑imperialist traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the work's role in linguistic decolonisation: does it reclaim, develop, and dignify indigenous languages; contribute to national culture, mass literacy, and political emancipation? Recognise long‑term cultural and intellectual benefits (opening languages to philosophy, science, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'cultural bomb' / colonial alienation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The effect of the cultural bomb is to annihilate a people's belief in their names, in their languages..."; colonial alienation is the disassociation of conceptual/educational language from daily community language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a text contributes to the annihilation of indigenous cultural self‑belief or resists that process. Look for signs of linguistic disjunction (elite/formal vs everyday speech) and whether the work bridges or deepens that divide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and purpose (local/subaltern vs global readership)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of the writer's intended audience and purpose: to speak to a local/subaltern audience or to claim an international/global readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge literary choices (language, register, themes, distribution) against intended audience: is the aim to reach and empower a subaltern/mass audience, or to join world literature? Evaluate ethical and political implications of that choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of orature, indigenous theatrical and literary forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Orature and indigenous performance (e.g., open‑air theatre in Gikuyu) play a central role in transmitting culture and keeping languages alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess incorporation of oral traditions, performance practices, and community‑based modes of production as measures of cultural rootedness and accessibility. Anti‑pattern: privileging only print/Western formal modes to the exclusion of oral forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political role and commitment of the writer
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of the writer in a neocolonial nation is inherently political; writing choices are part of anti‑imperialist struggles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author's work explicitly or implicitly engages with anti‑imperialism, social justice, and empowerment of proletariat/peasantry. Consider whether literature is used as activism or as complicit cultural reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autobiographical/anecdotal method for accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of autobiography and anecdote lends accessibility to political/theoretical issues and acts as a bridge between reader and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether anecdotal elements effectively humanise theory, make complex ideas approachable, and foster empathy. Consider potential tradeoffs in theoretical rigor vs pedagogical reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical and empathetic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Decolonising the Mind provides an empathetic pedagogical framework useful for TESOL and for cultivating empathy for experiences of those learning English as a second language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a text's utility in pedagogy: does it broaden perspectives, correct Western‑centric absences, and serve as a resource for teaching language, literature, and cultural contexts?

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to material conditions alongside linguistic critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ insists that 'material circumstances must also change'—language critique should attend to material history (Marxist influence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work situates linguistic/political critique within material/economic context, or whether it fetishises language alone. Anti‑pattern: purely romantic/ahistorical claims about language without material analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic appropriation and creative deformation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is subversive potential in appropriating a colonist language by 'de‑forming a "standard" European tongue and re‑forming it in new literary forms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess innovative linguistic strategies that reshape hegemonic languages (lexical invention, syntax shifts, hybrid forms) as acts of resistance and creativity. Consider effectiveness and clarity for intended audiences.
